newsitem.title: USA: More Jamaica bauxite revamping needed - analysts.
newsitem.headline: More Jamaica bauxite revamping needed - analysts.

text.p: The decision by two Jamaican companies to merge their bauxite operations and jointly mine new deposits is a badly needed step to help secure the industry's long term future, but more rationalisation was still needed, analysts and officials said.

Last week Alpart and Jamalco announced they had signed a non-binding letter of intent to consolidate their bauxite mining operations on the South Manchester Plateau into a new mining company. Their alumina operations remain separate.
The final deal was due to be signed by year end, with the new company in place January 1998.
Jamalco is half owned by the government, the rest by Alcoa. Alpart is 65 percent owned by Kaiser Aluminum, and 35 percent held by Norsk Hydro.
"We envision beginning mining shortly after consolidation of the mining operations," a Kaiser spokesman said.

Parris Lyew-Ayee, general manager of the state-owned Jamaica Bauxite Institute, said the Jamalco-Alpart link up is one of several steps that will be needed to make the industry, a key moneyspinner, more competitive.
"It's a bold new step. It's not been tried before," Lyew-Ayee said.
Kaiser, in a joint Jamalco-Alpart statement also suggested more needed to be done.

"We believe that this consolidation presents an initial opportunity for the bauxite/alumina industry in Jamaica to address the challenges posed by rapidly increasing productivity and competition in the global marketplace."
Analyst Julian Kettle of Brook Hunt said one factor which has hindered investment in Jamaica's bauxite and alumina industry is the history of labor problems.
Lyew-Ayee said a leading labor union has come out in support of the Jamalco-Alpart rationalisation as a way to secure long term survival despite some "casualties" in the short-term.
Kaiser was unable to comment on possible job losses.

But some in the alumina industry believe that Jamaica's bauxite and alumina industry is already fatally flawed after the government introduced in the early 1970s a big levy on the industry, believing it could play an OPEC style role.
This sent investment dollars scurrying to bauxite and alumina projects in Australia and elsewhere, observers say.
Industry consultant Lester Chin said the Jamalco-Alpart venture will provide assistance that is badly needed at Jamalco and help the Jamaican bauxite industry overall.
"It won't return the Jamaica bauxite industry to a faster growth rate, but will avoid decline at Jamalco," Chin said.
Jamalco needs the bauxite from the South Manchester Plateau that can be processed using its low-temperature technology, Chin said.
Lyee-Ayew conceded that further rationalisation in the Jamaica bauxite industry, apart from shipping ports, was unlikely to happen until after the Jamalco-Alpart tie up was in operation.
Jamaica was on track, Lyee-Ayew said, to produce 12 million tonnes of bauxite and 3 million tonnes of alumina this year.
The key test for Jamaica's bauxite and alumina industry will be to attract investment for its North Coast Trelawny project, consultants and analysts said.
"I think the Trelawny project is doubtful," Kettle said. "Jamaica will become a major bauxite producer because of its low cost position." But Jamaica's outlook on the alumina said was the crux.
"They are not the most efficient in terms of production costs and that reflects the age of the plants. They have to improve productivity just to stand still," Kettle said.
((Huw Jones, New York Commodity Desk 212-859-1646))
